what: The chapter map of Gen ZX Developers, the GenAI Startup Edition, as rewritten for release candidate 2 from Dinis's proposal Gen ZX Developers (19 October 2026), which he told the librarian to run with: two generations (Z and X), the founder as the reader, the objective that by the end the reader has started a company, a new part Start the company at the centre, Building safely rebuilt as Build it without a server, four more hands-on chapters, and a measure. The rc1 map is kept as chapters-rc1.json so the two can be compared on the rounds page. gravity: the centre of gravity the chapter leans to; character: the cast member it is written for first; since: the candidate that first had the chapter; draft: its page in the current candidate.

states.storyboarded: a storyboard exists for its part
states.drafting: a chapter of it exists in the release candidate (v2/content/), written from its ideas; the board and Dinis decide what happens next
states.reviewed: the reviewer and synthetic readers have had a round

chapters.title: Gen ZX: who this book is for, and what it is for
chapters.punchline: Two generations, Z entering the workforce and X the subject-matter experts starting companies, often their parents; together Gen ZX, back to the ZX Spectrum; one objective, that by the end you have started a company; and the measure, the companies created.
chapters.note: New in rc2, from Gen ZX Developers.

chapters.title: You are lucky to be here
chapters.punchline: Wonder, not fear: you are starting out in the biggest change of your career, while the pieces are still landing. Spoken to both generations.

chapters.title: Everything is connected: graphs
chapters.punchline: A graph is a network, not a diagram: the detective's board, a map as a graph with positions, graphs of graphs, provenance as a graph, and start anywhere.
chapters.note: Placed just before Where do you land because a map is a graph with positions; whether graphs come before Wardley maps or after is Dinis's question (Everything is connected, task 1). Dot Language and AST are examples inside it (task 3).

chapters.title: Where do you land?
chapters.punchline: Maps before names, and the first thing to work out is your centre of gravity: explorer, villager or town planner.

chapters.title: Connect the dots backwards
chapters.punchline: Your path only makes sense looking back; learning is a lifelong skill you can finally shape to how you think; read this on paper.

chapters.title: What generative AI is
chapters.punchline: AI is a huge bucket; this book is about the kind that generates; how a language model works in plain words, why a better prompt helps, where hallucinations come from, and where Dinis was corrected.

chapters.title: Lenses, roles and loops
chapters.punchline: The second half of the explanation: a prompt is a lens, a role is a model with a description, an agent is a loop with a goal, tools are requests the model sends back, the model remembers nothing, long chats are compressed, so work in focused threads.
chapters.note: Placed right after What generative AI is, as the article asks (task 1).

chapters.title: Everyone who can brief an agent is a developer
chapters.punchline: The definition widened, and so did the door; here is what the briefing-only developer still cannot do.

chapters.title: Explorer coding, not vibe coding, and the handover
chapters.punchline: What people call vibe coding is exploration, and the word should say so: build to find out, then hand it to the people who will make it something others rely on; the founder's way of building, and both halves.

parts.title: Getting the job, or making it

chapters.title: Hired for the workflow
chapters.punchline: The one competitive advantage in 2026 is running agentic workflows; you are more technical than you think; it starts with the application.

chapters.title: Act as the job you want
chapters.punchline: If you are looking for a job you have time: do the job in public before you have it, make it linkable, put your CV online. The 2018 Be a founder as then and now: act like a founder then, be one now.

chapters.title: Publish, publish, publish: your own newsroom
chapters.punchline: A publishing loop you can copy on day one; small finished pieces; an article behind every answer.

chapters.title: Your first workspace
chapters.punchline: From a spreadsheet to a folder per person, in an afternoon; drafts never send; and why your agents should not run on your laptop.

chapters.title: How to work with agents
chapters.punchline: An agent is a session with a focus; the brief is the unit of work; one shared state across voice, chat and phone; and the trap of a rule per mistake.

chapters.title: Direction is the scarce skill
chapters.punchline: When anyone can build, choosing what to build, when to stop, and where a person belongs is what gets paid for; agents decide, people answer.

chapters.title: Facts, evidence and the record
chapters.punchline: Make fact-based decisions, as the cover says: count rather than remember, let the record check you, distrust self-reports.

parts.title: Start the company
parts.note: New in rc2: the centre of the startup edition. Six chapters from the founder to the company itself; the company chapters are from experience, not legal or tax advice, and three of them wait on Dinis's gap articles (the UK company, Lithuania, Portugal, the EU, the first customers).

chapters.title: Be a founder: the expert founders
chapters.punchline: Execution just got cheap: the person who spent twenty years inside a problem can now build the first version of the answer themselves, with agents; a third of new US startups have a single founder, and the fastest-growing founders average 45.

chapters.title: Ship it, and see if they miss it
chapters.punchline: Not to plan, not to pitch, not to architect: ship; give it away, and if they do not miss it, try again; the miss-it test applied to your users and to yourself.

chapters.title: Price it, then give it away
chapters.punchline: Free is never free for the other side: set the price first, then the early-access offer; pay after the value, and let what a page was worth set its price.

chapters.title: Sell
chapters.punchline: Selling a service before the product, a marketplace of people, the SaaS buyer's inertia, and due diligence done by sending an agent rather than a spreadsheet.

chapters.title: Fund it, or do not
chapters.punchline: Profitable before raising; sell founder shares or lend rather than issue; the controllable founder and what investors buy; the company you keep control of.

chapters.title: The company itself: the UK, Portugal, Lithuania, the European Union
chapters.punchline: How to actually do it, for real: a limited company in the UK, the case for Lithuania, Portugal and what it costs to run a small company there, the EU and its programmes, the cloud providers and the startup programmes that exist right now; from experience, not advice.
chapters.note: Waits on the journalist's gap articles; written in rc2 as its title, its ideas and what is missing.

parts.title: Build it without a server
parts.note: Was Building, safely in rc1; rebuilt around shipping serverless, from Gen ZX Developers.

chapters.title: Serverless, for real
chapters.punchline: If it bills you by the hour when nobody is using it, it is not serverless: no servers of yours with logic in them, no database, the file system as the database, a client-side product on static hosting, and a billing model to match; a founder with no servers has nothing to run at three in the morning.

chapters.title: Privacy by design: SG/Send, sgit, and the value of constraints
chapters.punchline: Data encrypted on the user's device, on a server that cannot read it; zero-knowledge vaults and where the keys live; the constraint that designs the product and what it does not remove (GDPR); European sovereignty as moving the cloud, not the code.

chapters.title: Controlling your agent: RiskMandate
chapters.punchline: Mandate, reach and the gap; hope versus enforcement; code is a liability; secrets never in the chat; learning to hack is still how you learn. A policy beside the prompt; the behaviour policy is the business logic; the ten questions.

chapters.title: Open source
chapters.punchline: Nobody can lock you in; the fork next door; your first pull request. Open source is not free: who pays for what your startup runs on.

chapters.title: Shipped means the user has it
chapters.punchline: Green does not mean live; tests that never run are not tests; go slow to go fast; five people who do not exist.

chapters.title: Graphs, memory and your future self
chapters.punchline: Memory is context management: many memories, fractal, published and shared; maintain knowledge rather than perfect it; keep your work linkable and backed up for the person you will be.

chapters.title: Civic responsibility
chapters.punchline: To hack means to solve problems; small countries can lead now that everyone can build; sovereignty is the ability to move. The EU and judo for small countries.

parts.title: Hands on, 2026
parts.note: Inside the book (decision 013), dated 2026 and renewed each year. Four chapters new in rc2 from Gen ZX Developers.

chapters.title: An agentic workflow from zero
chapters.punchline: One afternoon, five exercises: from a spreadsheet to a folder per person, and a first agent that works for you.

chapters.title: Your first graph, built by hand
chapters.punchline: Nodes, edges as verbs, and a first graph of something you know, after chapter 15 of Fractal Semantic Graphs.

chapters.title: One idea, five lenses
chapters.punchline: Explain one idea of your own choice for a teenager, a musician, a doctor, a football fan and in another language; see the lens, not the magic.

chapters.title: A tiny agent loop
chapters.punchline: A page of code, or a no-code version, that shows the loop and one tool call: do the task, are we done, go round again.

chapters.title: Images, infographics and storyboards, drawn by code
chapters.punchline: A storyboard is data; the picture is drawn in the browser; the quote is checked against its source.

chapters.title: Meeting briefs and follow-ups
chapters.punchline: A briefing for you, a briefing on who you meet, a follow-up after: the best-prepared person in the room, every time.

chapters.title: Your own newsroom and inbox
chapters.punchline: Voice memo in, a checked site out; the email workflow replicated: publishing and communication that scale.

chapters.title: Form your company
chapters.punchline: The steps to a limited company in the UK, and the first look at Lithuania and Portugal; what to decide before you register.
chapters.note: Waits on the gap article; written as what is known and what is missing.

chapters.title: The credits and programmes, 2026
chapters.punchline: The startup cloud credits and programmes as they stand this year (AWS, Microsoft, Google, Anthropic), what each asks for, and how long they last.

chapters.title: Your first price and your first ten customers
chapters.punchline: Set the price, make the early-access offer, ask after the value, and find ten people who would miss it.

chapters.title: Ship a serverless product in a weekend
chapters.punchline: Static hosting, a vault for the data, chat on a static site, a payment link and no server of yours: the smallest product that a stranger can pay for.

parts.title: How this book was made, and what you made

chapters.title: How this book was made, and what you made
chapters.punchline: The repository and the vault, the roles, the articles as briefs, the decisions, the graph, the loop; co-written with Claude, and the ratio shown. The measure: the companies created from it, and how to tell us.

left_out.note: kept as one chapter in the long game; the Portugal talks are the then-and-now, not a part of their own
